import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs
from funs import DSText

import spacy

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"

#| tags: [noclear]
docs_raw = (
    pl.read_parquet(ub + "data/imdb5k_pca.parquet")
    .select(c.id, c.label, c.text)
    .rename({"id": "doc_id"})
    .sort(c.doc_id)

    .head(100)
)
```

#| tags: [noclear]
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
```

### Questions

`docs_raw` holds 200 IMDb movie reviews, 100 labeled `"positive"` and 100 labeled
`"negative"`, each with a `doc_id` and the raw `text` of the review. Many of the
reviews still contain the characters `<br />`, an HTML line break left over from
the web pages they were scraped from.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save
it to a variable.

1. Using `docs_raw`, count the number of reviews with each `label`.

```{python}
(
    docs_raw
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
)
```

2. Count how many reviews contain the string `"<br />"`. Use
`c.text.str.contains("<br />").sum()` inside of `.select`.

```{python}
(
    docs_raw
    .select(n_br = c.text.str.contains("<br />").sum())
)
```

More than half of them do: 105 of the 200.

3. Replace every `"<br />"` in `text` with a single space, using
`c.text.str.replace_all("<br />", " ")` inside of `.with_columns`.

```{python}
(
    docs_raw
    .with_columns(text = c.text.str.replace_all("<br />", " "))
)
```

4. The block below is given. It saves the cleaned reviews as `docs` and then runs
the spaCy pipeline over them with `DSText.process()`, which returns one row per
token. The result is saved as `anno`. It takes a little while to run.

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
docs = (
    docs_raw
    .with_columns(text = c.text.str.replace_all("<br />", " "))
)

anno = DSText.process(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.text), nlp)
anno
```

Each row is one token. `sid` is the sentence number within the review and `tid` is
the token number within the sentence. `lemma` is the dictionary form of the token
and `upos` is its part of speech.

5. Filter `anno` to the first sentence of the first review (`doc_id` equal to
`"doc0001"` and `sid` equal to 1) and select the columns `tid`, `token`, and `upos`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.doc_id == "doc0001", c.sid == 1)
    .select(c.tid, c.token, c.upos)
)
```

The sentence is "In my opinion, this movie is not good." Even the comma and the
period are tokens, with the part of speech `PUNCT`.

6. Use the same filter, but this time select `token` and `lemma`. Which token has a
lemma that is different from the token itself?

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.doc_id == "doc0001", c.sid == 1)
    .select(c.token, c.lemma)
)
```

**Answer**: The token "is" has the lemma "be". The lemma is also lowercase, so "In"
becomes "in".

7. Count the number of tokens with each part of speech (`upos`) across the whole
corpus. Sort from most to least common.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .group_by(c.upos)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

Nouns are the most common, followed by punctuation and verbs.

8. Take the code from the previous question and draw it as a bar plot with
`geom_col`, with `upos` on the x-axis and the count on the y-axis. Add
`coord_flip()` so the labels are readable.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .group_by(c.upos)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .ggplot(aes(c.upos, c.n))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

9. Filter to the nouns (`upos` equal to `"NOUN"`), count the number of times each
`lemma` appears, sort from most to least common, and keep the first 10 rows with
`.head(10)`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.upos == "NOUN")
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(10)
)
```

The top two are `movie` and `film`, which is not a surprise in a set of movie
reviews.

10. Take the code from the previous question and draw it as a bar plot with
`geom_col` and `coord_flip()`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.upos == "NOUN")
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(10)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lemma, c.n))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)
```

11. Do the same as question 9, but for verbs (`"VERB"`).

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.upos == "VERB")
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(10)
)
```

`see` and `watch` are near the top, which again fits the subject.

12. Do the same as question 9, but for adjectives (`"ADJ"`).

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.upos == "ADJ")
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(10)
)
```

13. Instead of filtering on the part of speech, keep the tokens that are made of
letters and are not stop words, using `.filter(c.is_alpha, ~c.is_stop)`. Then find
the 10 most common lemmas.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha, ~c.is_stop)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
    .head(10)
)
```

Stop words are very common words like "the" and "and". Removing them leaves a list
that mixes nouns, verbs, and adjectives.

14. Count the number of tokens in each review. Sort from longest to shortest.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

15. Take the code from the previous question (without the sort) and draw a histogram
of the number of tokens with `.geom_histogram(bins=30)`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .ggplot(aes(c.n))
    .geom_histogram(bins=30)
)
```

Half of the reviews are under 185 tokens, but two are over 1,000.

16. Find the number of sentences in each review by taking the largest value of `sid`
with `c.sid.max()`. Sort from most to fewest sentences.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(n_sent = c.sid.max())
    .sort(c.n_sent, descending=True)
)
```

17. `anno` does not have the `label` column, but `docs` does. Join `anno` to
`docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label)` on `doc_id`.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
)
```

18. Take the code from the previous question, filter to the adjectives, and count
the number of times each `lemma` appears within each `label`. Sort by the count from
largest to smallest.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
    .filter(c.upos == "ADJ")
    .group_by(c.label, c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

19. Change the code from the previous question so that it keeps only the lemmas
`"good"` and `"bad"`. Use `c.lemma.is_in(["good", "bad"])` inside of the filter.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
    .filter(c.upos == "ADJ", c.lemma.is_in(["good", "bad"]))
    .group_by(c.label, c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
)
```

20. Take the code from the previous question and draw a bar plot with `geom_col`,
with `lemma` on the x-axis, the count on the y-axis, and the fill color given by
`label`. Pass `position="dodge"` to `geom_col` to put the bars side by side.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
    .filter(c.upos == "ADJ", c.lemma.is_in(["good", "bad"]))
    .group_by(c.label, c.lemma)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .ggplot(aes(c.lemma, c.n, fill=c.label))
    .geom_col(position="dodge")
)
```

21. "bad" is used mostly in negative reviews, but "good" shows up often in both.
Look back at the sentence from question 5. Why does a count of "good" not separate
the positive reviews from the negative ones?

**Answer**: A review can say "not good," as in the first sentence of `doc0001`. The
count only sees the word "good" and ignores the "not" in front of it. "good" appears
80 times in positive reviews and 65 times in negative ones.
